item.title: Composer Without PHP: Embedding vivacity in ePHPm
item.description: The pitch for ePHPm is one binary in place of php-fpm, nginx and Redis. There was always a hole in it though. To deploy a PHP app you still need to run composer install, and that drags PHP and composer.phar back onto the box, or into the container build, just for that one step. ephpm composer install now runs a pure-Rust, Composer-compatible installer called vivacity inside the ePHPm binary. One binary serves the app and installs its dependencies, and on Windows that works with no PHP installed at all. Getting it right took five upstream PRs, a fork, a docs rewrite that took back claims we’d already made, and teaching ephpm to pretend to be php.

item.title: Clustered SQLite in ePHPm, Part 3: CDC Over the Cluster Channel
item.description:
By the end of Part 2 ePHPm v0.7.0 ran exactly one SQLite engine, Turso, in process, for single-node and clustered mode alike. The sidecar was gone. What I skipped over is how a replica actually gets the primary’s writes, and what happens when the primary dies with data on it. That’s this post.

  • Part 1: Replication by sidecar with sqld
  • Part 2: Adding Turso
  • Part 3: CDC over the cluster channel (this post)

CDC from the engine itself

Turso has change data capture built in. Turn it on for a connection and every committed change lands in a turso_cdc table with a monotonically increasing change_id, the table, the rowid, and before/after images of the record. The primary tails that table and ships transaction batches. Replicas apply them. That’s the whole design, and it landed as an experimental path in #186 at the end of July, with the tailer and applier in litewire (litewire#10).

item.title: Calling Rust From PHP Without a Socket, Part 1: The Native Functions
item.description: ePHPm is a single Rust binary that embeds PHP, and it carries its own KV store and its own SQLite-backed database in the same process. For a long time the only way PHP code could reach that KV store was the same way it reaches Redis: open a TCP socket to the RESP listener ePHPm runs on localhost, encode a command, wait for the reply. That works, and every PHP Redis client in existence already speaks it, but it is a strange thing to do when the hash map you’re talking to lives a few pointers away in the same address space.

item.title: P99 From 280 ms to 58 ms by Making the Queue Fair
item.description: A third-party Laravel runtime comparison put ePHPm’s worker mode at the top on throughput, about 19% ahead of FrankenPHP on /api/static, and at the bottom of the fast group on tail latency: P99 of 157 ms against FrankenPHP’s 57 ms. Best throughput plus the fattest tail is a shape worth chasing, because fast execution can’t produce it. Making requests faster lowers the mean and the tail. Only waiting can pull them apart, and specifically, unfair waiting.

item.title: Stop Running PHP on tokio's spawn_blocking - Own Your Thread Pool
item.description: For most of its life, ePHPm ran every PHP request on tokio’s spawn_blocking pool. It works. It passes tests, it serves benchmarks fine, and it’s the first thing anybody reaches for when they need to call blocking code from async Rust. It’s also quietly wrong for a language runtime, in ways that only show up under overload or after a crash. Over the last three weeks it got replaced with a pool of OS threads that ePHPm owns, first behind a config flag, then as the default, and as of v0.9.0 the spawn_blocking engine is gone.

item.title: Clustered ACME in Production: Three Bugs That Took TLS Down
item.description: ePHPm gets its own certificates from Let’s Encrypt, and in a cluster only one node should be talking to the CA. The nodes elect an ACME leader over the shared KV store, the leader orders the cert, and everybody else installs it from KV. That all had unit tests and had worked on single nodes for months. Then I tried to move wildcard TLS termination for our preview environment off a separate proxy and onto the 3-node cluster itself, and in about two days it found three separate bugs that each took TLS down. None of them showed up in a unit test, and all of them are the kind of thing you only learn by putting the feature on real machines.

item.title: Middleware in PHP: Compiling It With elephc, Then Not Needing To
item.description: ePHPm middleware runs before PHP. It’s a small versioned C ABI, loaded with dlopen, that gets to look at a request and reject it before PHP boots or the request body is read. That’s the right shape for a gateway, and it’s the wrong shape for most PHP shops, who want to write their middleware in PHP. This is the story of compiling PHP into a native .so to fit that ABI, finding exactly where it broke, and then building the lane that should have existed in the first place.

item.title: Security and Performance Hardening of a Rust Database Proxy
item.description:
litewire is the piece of ePHPm that lets PHP apps talk MySQL to a SQLite file. I wrote about how it works and about the MySQL quirks WordPress depends on. This one is the less visible half of August: an audit pass on litewire, a multi-tenant mode that turned a database proxy into a security boundary, and a performance regression I shipped and then had to go find.

It’s written in Rust, so memory safety is supposed to be the part I don’t have to think about. It mostly is. The use-after-free in this story was in a dependency, and the worst bug wasn’t a memory bug at all.

item.title: Rolling Your Own KV Store Instead of Embedding Redis
item.description: Every PHP deployment I’ve run eventually grew a Redis. Sessions, the WordPress object cache, Laravel’s cache and locks, rate limiting. ePHPm is supposed to be one binary that replaces nginx + php-fpm + Redis, so it needed a cache in the box. I didn’t want to write one. This post is why I did anyway, how it’s built, the bug that sat in its eviction code from March until last month, and how it holds up against a stock Redis on the same machine with redis-benchmark doing the talking.

item.title: Requests That End Wrong: A 200 That Was Really a Crash
item.description:
The scariest response a server can send isn’t a 500. It’s a 200 that should have been a 500. A crash is loud: the pod restarts, an alert fires, somebody looks. A truncated page with a success status code gets cached by your CDN, the health check calls the box healthy, and a client parses half a document as if it were the whole thing.

ePHPm embeds PHP inside a Rust server, so we own the part of PHP that php-fpm normally owns: starting a request, running the script, and ending it. Over the last couple of months I’ve fixed three bugs that all live in that start-and-end code, and none of them were in the SAPI I/O callbacks (ub_write, read_post and friends) where you’d expect to find embed bugs. They were in the Zend request lifecycle and in TSRM teardown, which is code you never touch when you run PHP behind php-fpm.

item.title: Gossip-Based Clustering for PHP Apps
item.description: Most PHP developers never touch clustering primitives, and that’s by design. PHP is share-nothing: each request starts from zero, and anything shared lives somewhere else. Sessions go in Redis, cache goes in Redis or Memcached, locks go in Redis, and when you run two app servers the “cluster” is really two stateless boxes pointed at the same Redis. That works until Redis is the thing you’re trying not to run.

item.title: Building a Custom SAPI - How PHP Actually Talks to the Outside World
item.description: If you’ve only ever run PHP behind nginx you’ve probably never had to think about how echo reaches a socket. When you embed PHP, as ePHPm does, it’s the first thing you have to answer, and the answer is a SAPI. There is very little written about implementing one. Most of what I know came from reading sapi/cli, sapi/cgi and sapi/embed in php-src and then finding out which parts I’d misread. This is the write-up I wanted back in March.

item.title: SQLite as a Production Database via Protocol Translation
item.description: Most of the PHP sites I’d put on ePHPm don’t need a MySQL server. A brochure WordPress, an internal Laravel tool, a preview environment that lives for an afternoon. What they do need is something that looks like MySQL, because mysqli and pdo_mysql are the only database drivers their code has ever been pointed at. I mentioned this in the ePHPm pragmatism post as a one-paragraph “because”. This is the longer version, now that WordPress 7.0 and Laravel 13 both install and run end to end on it.

item.title: The Pragmatism of ePHPm - Every Decision Has a "Because" Behind It
item.description:
ePHPm tagged v0.1.0 this week, three months after the first commit. Before the feature list grows any further I want to write down how decisions get made on it, mostly for myself, because the easiest way to ruin a project like this is to let it turn into a checklist of things other projects have.

The pitch is simple: one binary that runs a PHP app with fewer moving parts than nginx + php-fpm + Redis + MySQL. Every feature has to trace back to that. If I can’t finish the sentence “this exists because…” with a real problem from running PHP in production, it doesn’t go in.

item.title: PHP Signal Safety - The Init Ordering Bug Nobody Warns You About
item.description:
Last week I wrote about why ePHPm embeds PHP from Rust and promised the signal bug its own post. Here it is. It’s the kind of bug where the fix is about ten lines and the explanation is the whole post, because nothing in PHP’s embed documentation (there’s barely any) tells you that initializing PHP has process-wide side effects that assume PHP is the only thing in the process.

item.title: Why Rust for PHP Embedding (Not Go)
item.description: Go is my primary language and has been for a long time, so when I started building ePHPm a few weeks ago the obvious move was to write it in Go. ePHPm is a PHP application server: one binary that embeds the real PHP interpreter (libphp, the Zend engine) and puts an HTTP server, TLS, a KV cache and a database proxy around it, so a PHP app doesn’t need nginx + php-fpm + Redis to run. FrankenPHP already proved the “PHP inside a Go web server” idea works, and it works well. I wrote it in Rust anyway. This post is the reasoning, the part of the design that Rust made easier and the part it didn’t, and some numbers I should have measured before I wrote the design doc instead of after.
